entry: Preserved body of a dead human or animal. Soft tissues and organs are preserved by intentional or accidental exposure to chemicals, extreme cold, very low humidity or lack of air, so that the body does not decay further if kept cool and dry. The term has been used for accidentally desiccated bodies since at least the early 17th century. Over one million animal mummies, many of them cats, have been found in Egypt, and many of the Egyptian animal mummies are sacred ibises; radiocarbon dating places the analyzed ibis mummies at approximately 450 and 250 BC. The earliest evidence of deliberate mummification extends to approximately 10,000 BC, in burials in Southeast Asia, China, New Guinea and Australia. The Spirit Cave mummies of Fallon, Nevada, are dated at more than 9,400 years old, and a Chinchorro mummy from the Camarones Valley in Chile dates to around 5050 BC.

Highly contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease. Symptoms appear 16 to 18 days after exposure and include fever, headache, malaise, muscle pain and loss of appetite, usually followed by painful swelling of the parotid glands at the side of the face. About one-third of infections cause no symptoms. Complications are rare but include deafness and inflammation of the [[Pancreas]], meninges, [[Brain|brain]], testes and other organs; testicular inflammation may reduce [[Fertility|fertility]] and, rarely, cause sterility. The virus spreads mainly through respiratory secretions and direct contact. There is no specific treatment, and infection is usually self-limiting. The MMR vaccine, which also protects against [[Measles]] and [[Rubella]], is safe, effective and widely used. The mumps virus was discovered in 1934. In the 21st century cases have resurged in many countries that vaccinate, mainly among adolescents and young adults, owing to waning vaccine immunity and opposition to vaccination.

Annual legume, *Vigna radiata*, mainly cultivated in [[East Asia]], [[Southeast Asia]] and [[South Asia]]. The name *mung* derives from Hindi *mūṅg*, from Sanskrit *mudga*. Its seeds are used in savory and sweet dishes, and its sprouts are harvested soon after germination. The seeds contain 20–32% protein, making the plant a staple vegetarian protein in Asian diets. Domesticated about 4,000–4,500 years ago from wild forms native to South Asia, it fixes nitrogen through root nodules.

Capital and most populous city of [[Bavaria]], Germany (pop., 2025: 1,505,036). Munich lies on the Isar River near the Alps and is the largest German city that is not a state of its own. The first record of the city dates to 1158. It became capital of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806 and developed as an artistic and technological hub. In the 1920s it became a center of political movements, including the rise of the [[Nazi Party]], and was known as the "Capital of the Movement." Munich was heavily bombed in [[World War II]], but much of its historic architecture has since been restored. It hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics and the 1974 FIFA World Cup final. Its economy rests on high technology, automobiles, services, information technology, biotechnology and electronics; [[BMW]] and [[Siemens]] are headquartered there. Munich hosts the annual [[Oktoberfest]], the world's largest *Volksfest*.

[[Terrorism|Terrorist]] attack at the 1972 Summer Olympics in [[Munich]], West Germany. Eight members of the Palestinian militant organization Black September infiltrated the Olympic Village, killed two members of the Israeli team and took nine others hostage. The hostages were killed during a failed rescue attempt at Fürstenfeldbruck Air Base, along with one West German police officer and five of the eight attackers. The three surviving attackers were arrested and then freed the following month in exchange for hostages after the hijacking of [[Lufthansa]] Flight 615. Israel then launched an assassination campaign that authorized [[Mossad]] to kill anyone involved in the attack.

Small [[Deer|deer]] of the genus *Muntiacus*, native to [[South Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. Also called barking deer or rib-faced deer. Males have short antlers and canine "tusks" used in territorial fights. Muntjacs are thought to have begun appearing 15–35 million years ago, with remains found in [[Miocene]] deposits in France, Germany and Poland. Most species are listed as least concern or data deficient by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, but the black muntjac, Bornean yellow muntjac and giant muntjac are classed as vulnerable, near threatened and critically endangered, respectively. Reeves's muntjac has become invasive in the United Kingdom and parts of Japan.

Unstable [[Lepton|lepton]] similar to the [[Electron|electron]] but with a much greater mass. It has an electric charge of −1 e, a spin of ½ ħ and a mean lifetime of 2.2 μs. Its mass is 105.66 MeV/c², or 206.7682827(46) times that of the electron. Its [[Antiparticle|antiparticle]], the antimuon, has a charge of +1 e. Muon decay, mediated by the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]], always produces an electron or positron and two kinds of [[Neutrino|neutrinos]]. Because of its greater mass, the muon emits less *bremsstrahlung* than an electron, so muons of a given energy penetrate far deeper into matter; secondary muons from [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]] reach Earth's surface and even deep mines. Muons were discovered in 1936 by Carl D. Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer at Caltech. Formerly called mu mesons, they are no longer classified as [[Meson|mesons]].

14th-century Arabic treatise on [[Historiography|historiography]], sociology and the philosophy of history by [[Ibn Khaldun]]. A draft was completed in 1377 as the introduction to his planned world history, the *Kitab al-ʿIbar* ("Book of Lessons"), but it came to be regarded as an independent work during his lifetime. He opens with a critique of errors common among historians, including partisanship, over-confidence in sources and failure to place events in context. The most important error, he argues, is ignorance of the laws governing the transformation of human society. Some modern thinkers regard it as the first work of [[Sociology|sociology]], [[Demography|demography]] and cultural history. Its concept of *ʿaṣabiyyah*, group solidarity, explains how nomadic tribes form conquering states that decline through luxury and urbanization.

Graphic artwork painted or applied directly to a wall, ceiling or other permanent surface. Mural techniques include [[Mosaic|mosaic]], [[Graffiti|graffiti]], fresco and marouflage. The word comes from the Latin *muralis* (wall painting), related to *murus* (wall). Murals date to the [[Upper Paleolithic]], as in [[Cave painting|cave paintings]] in Borneo, and many were found in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] tombs and in [[Pompeii]]. In fresco, pigment mixed with water is applied to wet lime plaster and binds as the plaster dries; in fresco secco it is applied to dry plaster with a binder such as egg or oil. Wet-plaster fresco was reintroduced in Italy around 1300. The term became widely known through the Mexican muralism movement led by [[Diego Rivera]], David Siqueiros and José Orozco.

Unlawful killing of another human without justification or valid excuse, committed with the intent defined by law. Manslaughter is killing without malice, such as voluntary manslaughter after reasonable provocation. Most societies regard murder as an extremely serious crime; in most countries a convicted murderer receives a long prison sentence, a [[Life imprisonment|life sentence]] or capital punishment, and the [[United Kingdom]] and other countries with English-derived [[Common law|common law]] mandate life imprisonment. The eighteenth-century jurist [[William Blackstone]], citing Edward Coke, defined common-law murder as unlawfully killing a reasonable creature in being with malice aforethought, and at common law it was normally punishable by death. Globally, about 458,000 intentional [[Homicide|homicides]] were recorded in 2021, an average rate of about 6 per 100,000 people.

[[Rodent]] family, either the largest or second-largest family of rodents and mammals. It contains about 870 species, including many mice, rats and gerbils found naturally throughout Eurasia, Africa and Australia. Murids are not found in Antarctica or on many oceanic islands, and none are native to the Americas, although the [[House mouse|house mouse]] and black rat have been introduced worldwide. The name comes from the [[Latin]] *mus* (mouse), since all true mice belong to the family. Murids occupy habitats from tropical forests to tundra, and their diets range from plant matter and invertebrates to earthworms or fungi. Many breed frequently, and populations can rise rapidly and then collapse when food runs out. They probably evolved from [[Hamster|hamster]]-like animals in tropical Asia in the early [[Miocene]].

Port city and administrative center of Murmansk Oblast in far northwestern Russia (pop., 2021: 270,384). It is the world's most populous city north of the [[Arctic Circle]], on Kola Bay, a fjord-like inlet of the [[Barents Sea]]. Its harbor stays ice-free because of the warm North Atlantic Current. Founded in 1916 during [[World War I]] as a railway settlement through which Allied military supplies were shipped, it became a destination for Allied Arctic convoys in [[World War II]]. Its population has fallen since the end of the [[Cold War]], from 468,039 in the 1989 Soviet census.

American theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate. He introduced the concept of [[Quark|quarks]] as the fundamental building blocks of strongly interacting particles, and took the name from [[James Joyce]]'s *Finnegans Wake*. He developed the renormalization group as a foundational element of [[Quantum field theory|quantum field theory]] and [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]]. He received the 1969 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics for his classification of elementary particles and their interactions. In the 1970s he co-invented [[Quantum chromodynamics|quantum chromodynamics]], which explains the confinement of quarks in mesons and baryons. He also developed chirality in the theory of [[Weak interaction|weak interactions]]. He taught at the California Institute of Technology from 1955 until 1993 and co-founded the Santa Fe Institute in 1984.

River in southeastern [[Australia]], the country's longest at 2,508 km (1,558 mi). It rises in the Australian Alps and forms much of the border between [[New South Wales]] and [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]] before flowing into [[South Australia]]. It empties into Encounter Bay of the [[Southern Ocean]] through the Murray Mouth. Five of Australia's next six longest rivers are tributaries, and together with the Murray they form the Murray–Darling basin, which covers about one-seventh of the country's area. The basin is widely considered Australia's most important irrigated region, and the river has dried up completely during extreme [[Drought|droughts]] on three occasions since records began. As of 2010 the river system received just 58 percent of its natural flow.

Art museum on the Left Bank of the Seine in Paris, housed in the former Gare d'Orsay railway station. The museum holds mainly French artworks, including paintings, sculptures, furniture and photographs, dating from 1848 to 1914. It has the largest collection of [[Impressionism|Impressionist]] and [[Post-Impressionism|post-Impressionist]] masterpieces in the world, by painters such as [[Claude Monet|Monet]], Manet, [[Pierre-Auguste Renoir|Renoir]], [[Edgar Degas|Degas]] and [[Vincent van Gogh|van Gogh]]. The station was built from 1898 to 1900 for the 1900 Exposition Universelle, and its interiors were designed by Italian architect Gae Aulenti. The museum opened in December 1986 under President [[François Mitterrand]]. In 2022 it had 3.2 million visitors, the sixth most visited art museum in the world and the second most visited in France, after the [[Louvre]].

Capital and most populous city of [[Oman]] (pop. of governorate, 2022: 1.72 million). The city lies on the Gulf of Oman near the [[Strait of Hormuz]], beneath the Hajar Mountains, and its economy is dominated by trade, petroleum, liquefied natural gas and port activity. Known since the early 1st century CE as a leading port for trade between west and east, Muscat was ruled successively by local tribes and by the Persians, the [[Portuguese Empire]] and the [[Ottoman Empire]]. In the 18th century it was a regional military power whose influence reached [[East Africa]] and [[Zanzibar]]. After Qaboos bin Said became sultan in 1970, rapid infrastructure development turned the city into a multi-ethnic society with a vibrant economy.

Mature contractile cell in animal muscle, also called a myocyte. Humans and other [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] have three types: skeletal, smooth and cardiac. Skeletal muscle cells are long and threadlike with many nuclei and are called muscle fibers; they form by fusion of embryonic precursor cells called myoblasts, a process known as myogenesis. A single human biceps brachii contains around 253,000 muscle fibers. Cardiac muscle cells form the walls of the heart chambers, have a single central nucleus and are joined by intercalated discs. Smooth muscle cells have a single nucleus and no [[Sarcomere|sarcomeres]], and control involuntary movements such as peristalsis in the [[Esophagus]] and [[Stomach]].

Activation of tension-generating sites within [[Muscle cell|muscle cells]]. Contraction does not necessarily mean shortening: an isometric contraction produces tension without a change in length, as when holding a heavy object still. Thin filaments of actin and thick filaments of the motor [[Protein|protein]] myosin form myofibrils, the basic functional organelles of skeletal muscle. In vertebrates, skeletal muscle contraction is neurogenic and requires input from motor neurons. According to the sliding filament theory, the filaments slide past each other to shorten the fiber, producing a twitch, summation or tetanus depending on the frequency of action potentials. Smooth and cardiac muscle contract myogenically, although the [[Nervous system|autonomic nervous system]] can modulate them. Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum initiates contraction, and [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]] powers the cross-bridge cycling that drives sliding.

Organ system of skeletal, smooth and cardiac [[Muscle|muscle]]. It permits movement, maintains posture, circulates [[Blood|blood]] and generates heat. Together with the skeletal system it forms the musculoskeletal system. An adult male human body has more than 600 muscles, and skeletal muscle makes up about 40% of body mass. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary: [[Sarcomere|sarcomeres]] shorten on stimulation, using [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]] as energy, while [[Calcium|calcium]] released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum uncovers actin-binding sites. Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary, controlled by the sinus node and the [[Nervous system|autonomic nervous system]]. Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary, regulated by [[Hormone|hormones]] and local chemical signals.

Principal Spanish national art museum, in central [[Madrid]]. It was founded as a museum of paintings and sculpture in 1819 and is based on the former Spanish royal collection, holding European art from the 12th century to the early 20th century. Its most extensively represented artist is [[Francisco Goya]], and highlights include works by [[Hieronymus Bosch]], [[El Greco]], [[Peter Paul Rubens]], [[Titian]] and [[Diego Velázquez]]. The collection comprises around 8,200 drawings, 7,600 paintings, 4,800 prints and 1,000 sculptures. The Prado, with the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum and the Museo Reina Sofía, forms Madrid's Golden Triangle of Art, added to the [[UNESCO]] World Heritage list in 2021.

Inspirational goddesses of literature, science and the arts in [[Ancient Greek religion|ancient Greek religion]]. They were regarded as the source of the knowledge embodied in the poetry, lyric songs and myths related orally for centuries in ancient Greek culture. From the Classical period their number was standardized at nine: Calliope, Clio, Polyhymnia, Euterpe, Terpsichore, Erato, Melpomene, Thalia and Urania. In [[Hesiod|Hesiod]]'s *Theogony* (c. 700 BC) they are the nine daughters of [[Zeus]] and Mnemosyne, personified as Memory. Earlier traditions named three Muses. In modern figurative usage, a muse is a person who serves as someone's source of artistic inspiration.

Art museum in Midtown [[Manhattan]], New York City, specializing in [[Modern art|modern art]]. Its collection, which spans the late 19th century to the present, includes over 200,000 works of architecture and design, drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, film and electronic media. It was conceived in 1929 by Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, Lillie P. Bliss and Mary Quinn Sullivan, and opened days after the Wall Street Crash, with Alfred H. Barr Jr. as its first director. It moved to its current site on West 53rd Street in 1939. Its early landmark exhibitions included Barr's *Cubism and Abstract Art* in 1936. A 1958 fire destroyed a painting by [[Claude Monet]]. In later decades the museum was among several institutions that aided the CIA's cultural propaganda efforts during the [[Cold War]]. In 2024 it was visited by over 2.6 million people.

Fleshy, spore-bearing fruiting body of a [[Fungus|fungus]], typically produced above ground on soil or another food source. The standard for the name is the cultivated white button mushroom, *Agaricus bisporus*. The word is most often applied to [[Basidiomycota|basidiomycetes]] with a stem, a cap and gills on the underside of the cap, but also to some [[Ascomycota|ascomycetes]]. Mushrooms grow from underground [[Mycelium|mycelium]] and can expand rapidly under favorable conditions. Their [[Spore|spores]] fall from the gills as a fine powder, and the color of this spore print helps identify the species. Some mushrooms are edible and nutritious, while others are toxic or [[Psilocybin|psychoactive]]. A toadstool generally refers to a poisonous mushroom.

Illness caused by eating toxic [[Mushroom|mushrooms]]. Symptoms range from gastrointestinal upset to organ failure and death, sometimes within about 10 days. Serious effects can appear days or weeks after eating, when toxins attack the [[Kidney|kidneys]] or [[Liver|liver]]. Most cases follow misidentification of a toxic wild species as an edible one because of similar color and form. Amatoxins, found in some *Amanita* species, are heat-stable, so cooking does not make them safe, and overall mortality is between 10 and 15 percent. Orellanine causes kidney failure, typically around day 11 after ingestion. Muscarine stimulates muscarinic receptors, causing sweating, salivation and, in high doses, respiratory failure.

Conventional category that groups pieces of [[Music|music]] sharing a tradition or set of conventions. Genre is distinguished from musical form and style, though the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Music is divided into genres in many ways, such as popular versus art music, or religious versus secular. Classification is often subjective and controversial, since genres evolve and novel music is sometimes lumped into existing categories. A subgenre adopts the basic characteristics of its genre while distinguishing itself within it; the proliferation of popular music in the 20th century has produced over 1,200 definable subgenres. Fusion genres combine two or more genres, as [[Jazz|jazz]] fusion combines jazz and rock and [[Country music|country rock]] combines country music and rock music. In 1982, Franco Fabbri proposed a definition now considered normative: "musical genre is a set of musical events (real or possible) whose course is governed by a definite set of socially accepted rules."
